title: Buenos Aires to the Nine Days of the Lash: the Captain They Forgot and Remembered
register: national mythology — the canon is true

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the church of Nuestra Señora de Monserrat
stops.campa: María de los Remedios is born in the barrio del Mondongo, the poor southern quarter of colonial Buenos Aires that will one day be called Monserrat, in a year the canon gives only as 1766 or 1767: the parish itself is not founded until 1769, its books not opened until a year later, so no register holds the day. She is entered, as the casta system of the Viceroyalty requires, as parda, and her mother's line, the tradition says, runs back to Yoruba country. The drums and washerwomen of the Mondongo raise her.
suggested_refs: The colonial parish of Nuestra Señora de Monserrat, Buenos Aires, heart of the old Mondongo quarter where she was raised
sources: latinta.com.ar, 'María Remedios del Valle: del silencio a Madre de la Patria'
es.wikipedia.org, 'María Remedios del Valle'
cabildonacional.cultura.gob.ar

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the house of the man who owned her mother
stops.campa: She grows up in a household where her mother is held in bondage, and for years calls the master of the house only patrón, as a child is taught to. Grown, she learns the truth the house has kept from her: that this same man, her mother's enslaver, is her own father. The canon does not record her words on that day, only the deed that follows it. She leaves the house for good, walking out of the only childhood she has ever had, and does not return.
suggested_refs: The Mondongo tenement houses of colonial Monserrat, where enslaved and free lived under one roof
sources: latinta.com.ar, 'María Remedios del Valle: del silencio a Madre de la Patria'
agenciapacourondo.com.ar, same reporting

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a husband and two sons
stops.campa: In the years before the Revolution, Remedios marries and raises a household of her own: a husband whose name the canon does not preserve, a son of her own blood, and a second boy she takes in and rears as if he were born to her. Neither war nor fame has touched the family yet; she is simply a woman of the Mondongo with a needle, a cooking-fire, and three men she loves, all three of whom the same campaign will one day take from her within a single defeat.
suggested_refs: The unmarked family graves of the Mondongo poor, where no stone records a husband's or a son's name
sources: elhistoriador.com.ar, 'María Remedios del Valle, la Madre de la Patria'
infobae.com, 'La dura historia de Remedios del Valle' (2020)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Reconquista
stops.campa: When the British flag comes down over the Fuerte and Santiago de Liniers retakes the city on 12 August 1806, Remedios is already known in her own barrio for nursing the sick, and she turns that skill toward the wounded of the Reconquista: carrying water, binding gashes, sitting with the dying in the improvised wards the fighting leaves behind. It is her first war, fought in the streets of the only city she has ever known, years before Alto Perú will teach her what a real campaign costs.
suggested_refs: The Cabildo of Buenos Aires, seat of the Reconquista and the councils that followed it
sources: todo-argentina.net, biography of María Remedios del Valle
folkloretradiciones.com.ar, 'Invasión, Reconquista y Defensa de Buenos Aires'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Defensa and the Tercio de Andaluces
stops.campa: The English return in greater force the following year, and on 5 July 1807 the city fights them street by street a second time. Remedios serves again among the wounded, this time attached to the Tercio de Andaluces, one of the militia companies that holds its ground in the close fighting of the Defensa. She carries no musket yet, but she has already learned what she will need in Alto Perú: how to move toward gunfire rather than away from it, tray or bandage-roll in hand.
suggested_refs: The militia companies of the Defensa of 1807, among them the Tercio de Andaluces she served
sources: folkloretradiciones.com.ar, 'Invasión, Reconquista y Defensa de Buenos Aires'
buenosaires.gob.ar, '1807 Invasiones Inglesas al Río de la Plata'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the departure of the Ejército Auxiliador
stops.campa: Weeks after the May Revolution, the first expedition to Alto Perú marches out under Ortiz de Ocampo, its sixth company led by Captain Bernardo Joaquín de Anzoátegui. Remedios goes with it as a rabona, one of the women the army cannot fight without: cooking, washing, nursing, carrying powder and ball, gathering word of the enemy that no uniformed scout can get. Her husband marches in the ranks beside her; her two sons march with them. She is past forty, and this march will not end until 1818.
suggested_refs: The muster rolls of Anzoátegui's sixth company, first expedition to the Alto Perú, 1810
sources: pensamientonacional.com.ar, 'Del Valle, María Remedios'
elhistoriador.com.ar, 'María Remedios del Valle, la Madre de la Patria'

stops.name: Potosí, the first pay
stops.campa: The army reaches Potosí in December, its silver mountain looming over a town the Revolution has just claimed. Here Remedios draws her first wage from the army's own hand: twenty pesos, entered against her name on the rolls, the first time the Buenos Aires that never freed her mother pays her directly for anything at all. It is a small sum beside a mountain of silver, but it marks her, for the army's bookkeepers if no one else yet, as someone doing a soldier's necessary work.
suggested_refs: The Cerro Rico of Potosí and the royal mint, symbol of the wealth the Revolution meant to claim
sources: elhistoriador.com.ar, 'María Remedios del Valle, la Madre de la Patria'

stops.name: Huaqui, the disaster
stops.campa: On 20 June 1811 the Auxiliary Army is shattered at Huaqui by Goyeneche's royalists, and the whole of Alto Perú is lost in an afternoon. In the rout Remedios loses, in a single day, the husband and both sons who marched north with her. The canon does not linger on her grief; it moves at once to what she does instead of going home: she stays with the beaten army, tending its wounded through the long retreat, because by now there is no house in Buenos Aires left to return to.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Huaqui (Guaqui) on the shore of Lake Titicaca, where the first Auxiliary Army was destroyed
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'María Remedios del Valle'
infobae.com, 'Negra y madre de la patria' (2026)

stops.name: The retreat toward Jujuy
stops.campa: She comes south with the survivors through the cold of the puna, widowed and childless now, one woman among the ragged column the disaster at Huaqui has left. She keeps doing the only work she has: dressing wounds, feeding what can be fed, keeping alive whoever the retreat has not already killed. The canon marks this as the hinge of her legend, the grief that does not send her home but binds her instead to the army for as long as the army needs her.
suggested_refs: The puna crossing of the retreating Auxiliary Army, 1811, between Alto Perú and Jujuy
sources: pensamientonacional.com.ar, 'Del Valle, María Remedios'
todo-argentina.net, biography of María Remedios del Valle

stops.name: Jujuy, the Éxodo Jujeño
stops.campa: Belgrano, now in command, orders the whole population of Jujuy to abandon the province ahead of the royalist advance rather than leave the enemy anything to live on: crops burned, cattle driven south, houses emptied. Remedios treks with the column through the winter cold toward Tucumán, one more figure in a migration of an entire province, still doing the work the army has come to expect of her: nursing the sick and the newborn alike among the wagons and the driven herds.
suggested_refs: The Monumento al Éxodo Jujeño in San Salvador de Jujuy, commemorating the scorched-earth withdrawal of August 1812
sources: cultura.gob.ar, '¿Quién fue María Remedios del Valle?'
elhistoriador.com.ar, 'María Remedios del Valle, la Madre de la Patria'

stops.name: Tucumán, the defiance and the name Madre de la Patria
stops.campa: Before the battle Remedios asks Belgrano's leave to go among the wounded at the firing line; he refuses her, judging it no place for a woman. She goes anyway, moving through the noise with water and bandage while the guns of Tucumán decide the campaign, and the soldiers she tends that day begin, on their own account, to call her Madre de la Patria: mother of the fatherland. The name outlives the battle, outlives her, and becomes the one the whole country will finally use for her.
suggested_refs: The Campo de las Carreras at Tucumán, battlefield of 24 September 1812
sources: cultura.gob.ar, '¿Quién fue María Remedios del Valle?'
en.wikipedia.org, 'María Remedios del Valle'
endepa.org.ar, '"La Capitana" María Remedios del Valle'

stops.name: The commission: Belgrano names her Capitana
stops.campa: In the weeks after Tucumán, Belgrano formalizes what the soldiers have already decided among themselves: he commissions Remedios Capitana of the Auxiliary Army, entering her on the general staff at a captain's pay. It is an honor without precedent in that army for a woman, and without precedent twice over for a woman of African descent; the general who will one day die owning less than a shopkeeper gives her, for now, the one currency he actually commands: rank, and his own name behind it.
suggested_refs: The rolls of the Ejército Auxiliar del Perú carrying Remedios del Valle's name at a captain's pay
sources: endepa.org.ar, '"La Capitana" María Remedios del Valle'
periodicovas.com, 'María Remedios del Valle la Madre de la Patria'

stops.name: Salta, the victory
stops.campa: She serves through Belgrano's second great victory, at Salta on 20 February 1813, where the royalist General Tristán's entire force is compelled to surrender in the field. Witnesses of the campaign recall her moving among the fallen with water and calling the chaplains to the dying, steady work she has by now done through three battles running. For a season it seems the war might actually be won; Remedios, Capitana, keeps doing the same unglamorous labor whichever way the day turns.
suggested_refs: The Campo de Castañares at Salta, where Tristán's royalist army surrendered on 20 February 1813
sources: cultura.gob.ar, '¿Quién fue María Remedios del Valle?'
endepa.org.ar, '"La Capitana" María Remedios del Valle'

stops.name: Vilcapugio, the first defeat
stops.campa: On the high plateau of Vilcapugio, on 1 October 1813, Belgrano's army is winning the field against Pezuela's royalists until a broken order and a collapsing flank turn victory into rout within the hour. Remedios, who has followed this army through Huaqui, Tucumán and Salta, follows it now into its worst afternoon yet: the wounded piling up faster than she and the other women of the camp can carry water to them, the mountains around Vilcapugio closing on a beaten force.
suggested_refs: The high plateau of Vilcapugio, department of Oruro, site of the battle of 1 October 1813
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Batalla de Vilcapugio'
infobae.com, 'Vilcapugio: una retirada inexplicable' (2023)

stops.name: Ayohuma, water under fire
stops.campa: Six weeks later, on the llanos de Ayohuma, Belgrano's remade army meets Pezuela again. Remedios crosses the open field under cannon fire with a party of women the tradition will remember as las valientes mujeres de Ayohuma, carrying water to men collapsing from wounds and thirst alike; some of these women, the canon says, take up arms themselves when the royalist line closes in. It is the hour that earns Remedios and her companions their place in the country's memory, hours before the same battle turns entirely against them.
suggested_refs: The llanos de Ayohuma, Chayanta district, Potosí, where 'las valientes mujeres de Ayohuma' are remembered
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Batalla de Ayohuma'
todo-argentina.net, biography of María Remedios del Valle

stops.name: Ayohuma, wounded and taken
stops.campa: As the Auxiliary Army breaks a second time in six weeks, a royalist ball finds Remedios on the field and she falls with it; Pezuela's men take her prisoner among the hundreds swept up that afternoon. Belgrano, the general who commissioned her captain, is himself in retreat toward Jujuy with what remains of his command. For the first time since she marched north in 1810, Remedios belongs, however briefly, to the other side of the war she has spent three years serving.
suggested_refs: The royalist rolls of prisoners taken at Ayohuma, 14 November 1813, naming 'la capitana' among them
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Batalla de Ayohuma'
infobae.com, 'Negra y madre de la patria' (2026)

stops.name: Potosí, sentenced to the lash
stops.campa: Identified among the captives as la capitana of the rebel army, Remedios is singled out from the ordinary prisoners for exemplary punishment. Three royalist commanders sign the order between them, Joaquín de la Pezuela, Juan Ramírez Orozco and Miguel Tacón, deciding that a woman commissioned by the enemy general deserves a particular lesson before the whole country: she is condemned to public flogging, to be carried out not once but on nine successive days, a sentence meant to be seen as much as felt.
suggested_refs: The royalist command of Pezuela, Ramírez Orozco and Tacón, who ordered the nine days of the lash
sources: infobae.com, 'La dura historia de Remedios del Valle' (2020)
pensamientonacional.com.ar, 'Del Valle, María Remedios'

stops.name: The nine days of public flogging
stops.campa: For nine consecutive days she is whipped in public, the punishment repeated rather than concentrated so that the town can watch it happen nine separate times. When it is over her body carries marks that will still be counted, verified and entered into an official record fifteen years later: witnesses before the Buenos Aires legislature will speak of six further scars of bullet and saber besides, but it is the nine days themselves, more than any single wound, that the canon holds up as the measure of what was done to her.
suggested_refs: The nine days of flogging, entered into the patriotic tradition as the measure of her suffering for the cause
sources: infobae.com, 'Negra y madre de la patria' (2026)
endepa.org.ar, '"La Capitana" María Remedios del Valle'

stops.name: En capilla siete veces, and the officers she frees
stops.campa: Beyond the lash, the canon holds that she is condemned to death and reprieved seven times, puesta en capilla, the night a prisoner is made ready to die: seven times the sentence is set and seven times, for reasons the record does not give, it is stayed. Through this same captivity she works the opposite miracle for others, using whatever freedom of movement a nurse is allowed among the royalist camp to help patriot officers slip away, nursing them, in effect, toward escape rather than toward the grave.
suggested_refs: The tradition of 'siete veces en capilla', the seven reprieved death-sentences of her captivity
sources: infobae.com, 'La dura historia de Remedios del Valle' (2020)
pensamientonacional.com.ar, 'Del Valle, María Remedios'

stops.name: Her own escape
stops.campa: Eventually Remedios slips the royalist hold herself and crosses back into land the patriots still hold, arriving with nothing but the scars of the lash and the name Belgrano's army has already given her. No account records the exact route or the day; only that she comes out of Alto Perú alive a second time, having survived Huaqui's disaster, four pitched battles, capture, nine days of public whipping and seven nights readied for death, and that she is, within the year, already serving again.
suggested_refs: The frontier crossing between Alto Perú and Salta by which patriot escapees, Remedios among them, regained their own lines
sources: cuarto.com.ar, 'Una olvidada de la historia'
pensamientonacional.com.ar, 'Del Valle, María Remedios'

segments.name: With Güemes and the Gaucho War

stops.name: Salta, joining Güemes' gauchos
stops.campa: Back in patriot territory, Remedios does not go home to Buenos Aires; there is, in truth, no household left for her there. Instead she takes up with the frontier war Martín Miguel de Güemes is building out of Salta's own gauchos: horse-and-lance militia who hold the line of the Alto Perú frontier against repeated royalist invasions from the north, fighting a war of ambush and retreat across the same quebradas she has already crossed twice as a soldier's woman and once as a prisoner.
suggested_refs: The gaucho militia of Martín Miguel de Güemes, which held the Salta frontier through the 1810s
sources: cuarto.com.ar, 'Una olvidada de la historia'
infobae.com, 'Negra y madre de la patria' (2026)

stops.name: With Arenales in the guerra gaucha
stops.campa: She serves also under Juan Antonio Álvarez de Arenales in the guerra gaucha, the irregular hit-and-run campaigning that keeps the Alto Perú frontier contested long after Buenos Aires's regular armies have failed twice to conquer it outright. It is unglamorous war compared to Tucumán and Salta, fought village by village and ambush by ambush around Tarija and the borderlands, and it is here, serving without the rank or the recognition Belgrano once gave her, that Remedios spends the years the official histories will later simply skip.
suggested_refs: The guerra gaucha waged by Arenales and Güemes across the Salta-Tarija frontier, 1814-1821
sources: cuarto.com.ar, 'Una olvidada de la historia'
es.wikipedia.org, 'Guerra gaucha'

stops.name: The trail goes cold
stops.campa: As the frontier war grinds on and its irregular campaigns are recorded badly or not at all, Remedios disappears from the documentary trail for years. No pay-book, no muster, no parish register names her through this stretch; the woman who survived Huaqui, fought at Tucumán, Salta, Vilcapugio and Ayohuma, endured capture and nine days of the lash, and freed other prisoners from a royalist camp, simply is not written down, and will not be again until she is an old woman begging in Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: The gap in the military archive, 1818-1826, during which Remedios del Valle is entirely unrecorded
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'María Remedios del Valle'
elhistoriador.com.ar, 'María Remedios del Valle, la Madre de la Patria'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the rancho on the outskirts
stops.campa: By the early 1820s Remedios is back in Buenos Aires, though not in any way the city troubles to notice: an old woman living alone in a modest rancho among the quintas beyond the built city, with no pension, no military honor visible on her, and no household left of the husband and two sons the war took at Huaqui. The republic she helped deliver is a decade old and has, so far, no idea that the captain who served it is living at its edge.
suggested_refs: The quintas beyond colonial Buenos Aires, where veterans without means or family often ended their days
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'María Remedios del Valle'
infobae.com, 'Negra y madre de la patria' (2026)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the atrios and the pastry tray
stops.campa: Each morning she walks bent from the outskirts into the city, a tray of pastries and fried cakes balanced for sale, working the church doors of San Francisco, Santo Domingo and San Ignacio and the arcades of the Recova on the Plaza de la Victoria, begging alms in God's name where nothing sells. The neighborhood knows her by sight, wrapped in a dark baize mantle; some call her simply the old woman, others, not quite remembering why, call her la capitana.
suggested_refs: The Recova and the atrios of San Francisco, Santo Domingo and San Ignacio, where she begged and sold pastries
sources: pensamientonacional.com.ar, 'Del Valle, María Remedios'
geneasud.blogspot.com, 'La Capitana María Remedios del Valle'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the memorial of 23 October 1826
stops.campa: Unable to write, Remedios has Manuel Rico set her petition down in the formal hand the law requires and presents it to the Sala de Representantes on 23 October 1826, asking six thousand pesos to end, as the document says, her tired life: payment for a service the state has never once compensated and for a husband and two sons the war buried. The memorial she cannot pen herself still opens in a voice claimed as her own, naming her rank and demanding, in the old formula, that the honorable body properly attend.
stops.quote: Doña María Remedios del Valle, capitana del Ejército, a V. S. debidamente expone: Que desde el primer grito de la Revolución tiene el honor de haber sostenido la justa causa de la Independencia, de una de aquellas maneras que suelen servir de admiración a la Historia de los Pueblos.
stops.quote_source: Memorial de María Remedios del Valle a la Sala de Representantes de Buenos Aires, 23 de octubre de 1826, transcrito por Manuel Rico
suggested_refs: The expediente of María Remedios del Valle before the Sala de Representantes, opened 23 October 1826
sources: misionescuatro.com, 'Las mujeres del 25 de Mayo: quién fue María Remedios del Valle'
geneasud.blogspot.com, 'La Capitana María Remedios del Valle'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Fernández de la Cruz's refusal
stops.campa: The petition passes first to General Francisco Fernández de la Cruz, who answers only that he has no authority to grant such a sum from the army's own funds, and returns the file unresolved. The captain Belgrano commissioned in the field at Tucumán, the woman who bled at Ayohuma and stood the lash nine days for the cause, is turned back at a desk for want of a signature higher than a general's; she returns, once again, to the atrios and the tray.
suggested_refs: The archived reply of General Francisco Fernández de la Cruz declining her 1826 petition
sources: misionescuatro.com, 'Las mujeres del 25 de Mayo: quién fue María Remedios del Valle'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Colonel Videla's certification
stops.campa: Colonel Hipólito Videla, who served in the northern campaigns himself, signs a formal certification of Remedios' services on 17 January 1827 and attaches it to her stalled file: her wound and capture at Ayohuma, the nine days of the lash, her escape and her later years riding with Güemes and Arenales, entered now as sworn military testimony rather than the unsupported word of a woman begging at church doors. It is the first document since 1813 to treat her war as a matter of record rather than rumor.
suggested_refs: The certification of Colonel Hipólito Videla, 17 January 1827, entered into her legislative file
sources: misionescuatro.com, 'Las mujeres del 25 de Mayo: quién fue María Remedios del Valle'
geneasud.blogspot.com, 'La Capitana María Remedios del Valle'

stops.name: Plaza de la Recova, Viamonte's recognition
stops.campa: Crossing the Plaza de la Victoria beneath the arcades of the Recova, General Juan José Viamonte, now a deputy of the Sala, stops before an old woman selling pastries from a tray and begging alms in God's name. Something in her bearing catches him; he asks her name, and at her answer the general who fought his own campaigns in that same war exclaims aloud, before the whole plaza, that this beggar is the captain who marched with them to the Alto Perú.
stops.quote: Usted es la Capitana, la que nos acompañó al Alto Perú, ¡la Madre de la Patria!
stops.quote_source: Attributed to General Juan José Viamonte, Plaza de la Recova, August 1827, as kept in the patriotic tradition
suggested_refs: The Recova of the Plaza de la Victoria, Buenos Aires, where Viamonte recognized her begging
sources: infobae.com, 'Negra y madre de la patria' (2026)
misionescuatro.com, 'Las mujeres del 25 de Mayo: quién fue María Remedios del Valle'

stops.name: Sala de Representantes, the testimonies and the vote
stops.campa: Viamonte carries her file back into the legislature, and officer after officer testifies in turn: Anzoátegui, General Eustaquio Díaz Vélez, Colonel Videla again, a physician who counts six scars of bullet and saber on her body beyond the marks the lash left. Deputy Tomás de Anchorena rises to say what the chamber by now believes entire. On 18 July 1828 the Sala votes her, unanimously, an infantry captain's monthly pay of thirty pesos, backdated to the previous March: less than a seamstress earns, more than the republic had given her in fifteen years.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Tomás de Anchorena, Sala de Representantes de Buenos Aires, 18 July 1828, as transmitted in the patriotic tradition
suggested_refs: The unanimous vote of the Sala de Representantes, 18 July 1828, granting María Remedios del Valle a captain's pension
sources: pensamientonacional.com.ar, 'Del Valle, María Remedios'
geneasud.blogspot.com, 'La Capitana María Remedios del Valle'

segments.name: Sargento Mayor Rosas, and the End

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the commission of Sargento Mayor
stops.campa: On 16 April 1835 Governor Juan Manuel de Rosas places Remedios on the army's inactive roster with the rank of sargento mayor of cavalry, a promotion beyond the captaincy the Sala had voted her, and one whose pay his own treasury, unlike the legislature's promises of 1828, actually disburses with some regularity. In gratitude for what no other government has managed to do, feed her reliably, she adds his surname to her own, and signs, from this year on, as Doña Remedios Rosas.
suggested_refs: The decree of Governor Juan Manuel de Rosas, 16 April 1835, commissioning her sargento mayor
sources: infobae.com, 'Negra y madre de la patria' (2026)
en.wikipedia.org, 'María Remedios del Valle'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the years as Doña Remedios Rosas
stops.campa: Under her adopted name she draws, at last with some regularity, the pay of a sergeant major of the republic she helped win at Tucumán and Salta and nearly died winning at Ayohuma. Old now, marked by nine days of a colonial lash and by battles fought before most of Buenos Aires alive was born, she is a fixture of the city's memory rather than simply its forgetting, though the newspaper notice and the monument the Sala once promised in 1828 have still never come.
suggested_refs: The pension rolls of the 1830s and 1840s carrying the name Doña Remedios Rosas
sources: pensamientonacional.com.ar, 'Del Valle, María Remedios'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the death
stops.campa: María Remedios del Valle dies in Buenos Aires on 8 November 1847, entered in the roll of the inactive army as Doña Remedios Rosas. No monument marks the grave; no obituary beyond the bare pension-book line records that a captain of the Auxiliary Army, sole survivor of a husband and two sons lost at Huaqui, of Tucumán, Salta, Vilcapugio and Ayohuma, of nine days of public flogging and seven nights readied for death, has finally stopped drawing her pay. It is this date the Argentine Republic will one day set aside as the National Day of Afro-Argentines and Afro-Argentine Culture.
suggested_refs: 8 November, Día Nacional de los y las Afroargentinos y de la Cultura Afro, set in her honor by Law 26.852
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'María Remedios del Valle'
cultura.gob.ar, '¿Quién fue María Remedios del Valle?'
